The one metric that wasn’t included when I joined the enrollment data with the organizational data is the number of years they attended a school in the Southern region (as defined by the project).


enrollment.original <- read_csv("/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/K12 Enrollment/K12Enrollment.csv")  %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID),
         K12OrganizationID = as.integer(K12OrganizationID)) %>%
  drop_na(PersonID)

k12.org.original <- read_csv("~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/K12 Orgs/K12Organization-updated.csv") %>%
  distinct(K12OrganizationID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  drop_na(K12OrganizationID) %>%
  mutate(K12OrganizationID = as.integer(K12OrganizationID))

k12.org.master <- k12.org.original %>%
  select(K12OrganizationID, County, OrganizationName, DistrictID, SchoolNumber) %>%
  rename(county.name = 2) %>%
  mutate(county.name = str_replace(county.name, " County", "")) %>%
  select(K12OrganizationID, OrganizationName, county.name) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("county.name" = "Name")) %>%
  select(-Dem_RUCA, -mif, -edr.simple, -planning.region)

enrollment.org.central <- enrollment.original %>%
  left_join(k12.org.master, by = "K12OrganizationID") %>%
  filter(project.pr == "Southern")

n.years <- original %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, K12OrganizationID) %>%
  rename(grad.org.id = K12OrganizationID) %>%
  left_join(enrollment.original[,c(1,2,3,4)], by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.org.original[,c(1,2,3,7)], by = "K12OrganizationID") %>%
  mutate(year = str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, year, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarize(n.years.attended = n()) %>%
  ungroup()

master <- original %>%
  left_join(n.years, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Town/rural mix", "Urban/town/rural mix", "Entirely urban"))

title: K12Orgs
text:
Summary of high school location
Lets breakdown the graduates by which regions they graduated from.
Nearly half of students graduated from a county labeled as urban/town/rural mix, while 18% graduated from a town/rural mix, and 34% from an entirely urban county.








Below is a map with the percentages of graduates graduating from high schools located within each county. The schools with the highest percent of graduates/observations are located in Olmstead with 21% while all other counties ranged from 1.5% to 10% of the graduates.

title: K12Orgs
text:
Summary of student demographics
The following analysis looks to see if there are any statistical differences due to rural-ness and geographic location of the high school for the following graduate demographics;

Were eligible for free or reduced lunch at some point in the dataset
Are Female
Have been homeless at some point in the dataset
Had limited english proficiency at some point in the dataset
Had non english speakders in home at some point in the dataset
Participated in a PSEO course at some point in the dataset.

Lets start with the cross-tabs based on RUCA categories.
The cross-tabs below indicate that there are 4 demographic variables that have proportions statistically different across RUCA categories. Each of the variables are indicated with an asterisk.

Free or reduced lunch: a statistically significant higher percentage of graduates from high schools in entirely rural mix counties receive free or reduced lunch.
Homeless: as a school district becomes more urban, the percentage of it’s graduates indicating they experienced homeslessness at some point increases significantly.
PSEO: a siginficantly lower percentage of graduates from entirely rural districts participated in a PSEO program.


RUCA Free or Reduced LunchRUCA FemaleRUCA HomelessRUCA Limited EnglishRUCA non-english in homeRUCA PSEO


Although 30.2% of the total number of graduates in the data set receive free or reduced lunch, graduates from town/rural mix schools had significantly higher percentage with 33.2%.

---------------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
Urban/town/rural mix |     41153 |     17846 |     58999 |

---------------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|

Statistics for All Table Factors

------------------------------------------------------------

k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca <- master %>%
  group_by(Dem_Desc) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
           free.lunch = sum(economic.status)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = free.lunch / n,
         total.pct = sum(free.lunch) / sum(n),
         data_id = as.character(seq(n()))) 

k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca.plot <- ggplot(k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca, aes(Dem_Desc, pct, fill = Dem_Desc)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca$total.pct, color = "black") +
  geom_col_interactive(size = 5, aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(Dem_Desc, "\nTotal graduates: ", comma(n, accuracy = 1), "\nGraduates received free or reduced lunch: ", comma(free.lunch, accuracy = 1), "\nPercent of total graduates: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 3,
           y = k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca$total.pct,
           label = paste("All graduates\npercent, ", percent(k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca$total.pct, accuracy = .1)),
           size = 5) +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", fill = "", title = "Percent of graduates receiving free or reduced lunch")+
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_line+
  scale_fill_manual(values= color.ruca,
                     guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        text = element_text(size = 16))

  girafe(ggobj = k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca.plot) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
This research examined which factors most strongly influence whether individuals achieve meaningful employment within Southern Minnesota’s region (EDR 9 & 10) after high school. Using both contingency table analysis (effect sizes, trends over 1, 5, and 10 years) and CART modeling, the goal was to identify which variables most reliably anchor individuals in the regional workforce versus those that push them toward statewide mobility, disconnection, or outmigration.
A special focus was also placed on non-college graduates, who represent a substantial share of the region’s young adults and are at higher risk of disconnection from the labor force. Understanding their pathways provides additional insights into how to build a stronger, more inclusive regional workforce.
The findings provide a roadmap for education and workforce policy, showing how demographics, high school context, accomplishments, and postsecondary experiences interact to shape local labor market attachment.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Relationships - Employment

Total Summary
Across demographics, high school characteristics, accomplishments, and postsecondary experiences, clear themes emerge about what most strongly predicts meaningful employment in the region versus disconnection or statewide mobility.

Postsecondary experiences are the strongest predictors overall. Where a student graduates from, whether they graduate, and what credential they earn all have lasting effects on both regional retention and statewide opportunities.
Economic status and special education needs stand out among demographics as powerful predictors of early disadvantage and disconnection.
On the other hand, career and technical education (CTE) consistently boosts regional employment, making it a strong anchor to the local workforce.
Meanwhile, academic rigor variables (ACT, AP, MCA scores) largely point students toward postsecondary enrollment and careers beyond the region, signaling statewide mobility rather than regional attachment. Finally, some variables — particularly language indicators and one-off tests like SAT — show weak or inconsistent predictive value.




1. Strong Predictors of Regional Employment and Disconnection
These variables consistently show strong or moderate effect sizes and clear differences in meaningful regional employment, making them strong candidates for modeling.

More CTE courses = stronger regional employment attachment.






2. Moderate Predictors — Some Association, Less Consistency
These variables show moderate associations with outcomes. They may be useful in modeling, particularly when combined with other predictors.

Overall Conclusion
The most consistent predictors of regional workforce retention are sub-baccalaureate postsecondary pathways, public 2-year institutions, and CTE engagement, combined with rural high school origins. Meanwhile, academic rigor variables and 4-year degrees drive statewide mobility rather than regional employment. Disadvantage markers such as low-income status and special education needs are persistent risk factors for disconnection.
In short, the analysis reveals a dual pipeline:

CTE and 2-year credentials anchor students to Southern Minnesota’s workforce.
High academic achievement and 4-year+ credentials lead to mobility and employment beyond the region.

This suggests that interventions to strengthen the regional workforce should prioritize CTE pathways, 2-year institutions, and supports for low-income and special education students, while also recognizing that academic high-achievers are more likely to leave the region.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Relationships - Post-secondary
Across all four postsecondary outcomes — attended.ps, ps.grad, ps.grad.InstitutionSector, ps.grad.location, and highest.cred.level — consistent patterns emerge about which factors shape educational attainment and how these pathways tie into regional workforce retention versus mobility and disconnection.
The evidence is clear: postsecondary experiences are the strongest predictors of long-term employment outcomes, but they are deeply influenced by demographic background, high school context, and student accomplishments. This creates a dual-pipeline system: one that anchors students to Southern MN through CTE and sub-baccalaureate credentials, and another that channels academically strong students into statewide or national mobility through 4-year and higher pathways.


1. Attending Postsecondary Education

Key Predictors: Economic status (low-income less likely to attend), race/ethnicity (persistent gaps), and special education status (lower attendance).

Takeaway: Disadvantaged students are disproportionately less likely to enroll in PS at all, putting them at high risk of long-term disconnection.




2. Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)

Key Predictors: Economic status and SPED remain barriers to completion; racial gaps persist; academic readiness improves odds of graduating.

Takeaway: Simply completing PS dramatically reduces disconnection and boosts employment. Non-completers remain the most vulnerable group in the workforce pipeline.




3. Institution Sector of Graduation (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)

Key Predictors:

Academic rigor and PSEO → 4-year completions.

CTE engagement, SPED, and low-income → 2-year completions.


Takeaway: Institution type sorts students into applied versus academic pathways. Since 2-year completions are more strongly tied to regional employment, CTE and disadvantage groups inadvertently form the backbone of Southern MN’s workforce, while academically strong students pursue more mobile 4-year pathways.




4. Location of Graduation (ps.grad.location)

Key Predictors:

Disadvantaged students (low-income, SPED, marginalized race/ethnicity) → more likely to graduate in Southern MN.

High scorers and PSEO participants → more likely to graduate outside the region (other MN or out-of-state).

Local economic conditions (lower wages, higher unemployment) → stronger Southern MN completions.


Takeaway: Regional completions are most common among disadvantaged groups and CTE students, reinforcing their role in regional workforce stability.




5. Highest Credential Earned (highest.cred.level)

Key Predictors:

Academic rigor (ACT, MCA) and PSEO → bachelor’s or higher.

CTE engagement, low-income, SPED, disadvantaged counties → associate or sub-associate.


Takeaway: Credential level is the clearest stratifier of opportunity. Bachelor’s+ aligns with mobility, while associate/sub-associate aligns with regional employment.




Overall Conclusion
The postsecondary pipeline is shaped by two reinforcing forces:

Mobility Pipeline:

Driven by academic rigor and PSEO.
Leads to 4-year+ degrees, completions outside the region, and statewide mobility.
Most common among advantaged, higher-scoring students.

Regional Pipeline:

Driven by CTE engagement, 2-year institutions, economic disadvantage, SPED, and lower-wage/unemployment counties.
Leads to associate/sub-associate degrees and Southern MN completions, strongly tied to meaningful regional employment.
Most common among disadvantaged students who remain anchored locally.


In short: Southern MN’s workforce stability relies heavily on the regional pipeline of 2-year and CTE-driven pathways, which disproportionately serve low-income and SPED students. Meanwhile, academically strong and advantaged students pursue 4-year and higher credentials, fueling statewide and out-of-state mobility.
Policy Implication: To strengthen the regional workforce, interventions should both (1) support disadvantaged students in completing and leveraging their 2-year pathways and (2) create incentives for academically strong students to remain engaged in the region after completing higher degrees.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Prediction - Employment CART

Main takeaway
Across all three binary comparisons and all time horizons (1, 5, and 10 years after graduation), the CART models consistently highlight a dual pipeline shaping workforce outcomes in Southern Minnesota:

Anchors to Regional Employment:

CTE engagement and depth (≥2–5 courses, concentrator/completor status).
Sub-baccalaureate pathways (2-year credentials, certificates, some college).
Regional postsecondary attendance and graduation.
Favorable local economic conditions (competitive wages, lower unemployment).

Pathways to Statewide Mobility or Disconnection:

Bachelor’s degree attainment and high academic achievement (ACT ≥25–28, MCA Reading ≥4) consistently predict outward mobility into statewide labor markets.
Weak academic readiness (low ACT, low MCA scores) and lack of CTE engagement predict disconnection (no record, not attending PS).
Structural disadvantages (low-income, SpecialEd status, some racial/ethnic groups) persistently raise the risk of disconnection across all timeframes.


The synthesis underscores that CTE and regional postsecondary pathways are the backbone of workforce retention, while higher academic achievement and 4-year credentials lead to broader mobility. Disadvantaged groups remain at elevated risk of disconnection without targeted supports.



Year 1 after Graduation

Anchors: Early anchoring comes primarily from CTE engagement, math proficiency, and local labor market strength.
Barriers: SpecialEd involvement, weak academic readiness, and lack of CTE drive early disconnection or statewide mobility.
Interpretation: At this stage, exposure to CTE and basic academic preparation are critical to prevent graduates from being disconnected from work or education.




Year 5 after Graduation

Anchors: Regional postsecondary engagement, CTE depth, and sub-baccalaureate completion are most decisive.
Barriers: 4-year/Bachelor’s attainment predicts mobility out of the region; SpecialEd, gender, and racial disparities continue to shape risks of disconnection.
Interpretation: Mid-career, institutional pathways (regional PS, CTE credentials) dominate as anchors, while higher academic achievement channels students outward.




Year 10 after Graduation

Anchors: Long-term anchoring depends on regional postsecondary graduation, sustained CTE involvement, and competitive wage environments.
Barriers: Weak academic scores, lack of PS/CTE ties, and subgroup inequities push graduates toward disconnection or employment outside the region.
Interpretation: At this stage, outcomes stabilize: CTE and regional PS pipelines anchor students, while 4-year pathways and weak local wages reinforce outward movement or disconnection.




Overall Summary
The CART analyses converge on three central insights:

CTE engagement is the most consistent predictor of regional employment. Even minimal exposure is protective, while concentrator/completor status provides the strongest anchor.
Regional postsecondary pathways matter profoundly. Attendance and completion in Southern Minnesota institutions substantially increase the odds of regional employment at 5 and 10 years.
Mobility vs. disconnection split.

Mobility: High achievers and 4-year graduates are more likely to find meaningful employment statewide.
Disconnection: Students with weak academic readiness, limited CTE, and structural disadvantages face higher risks of no employment record or PS engagement.


This duality reflects a regional workforce pipeline rooted in CTE and 2-year credentials, contrasted with a mobility pipeline driven by academic achievement and 4-year degrees.



Policy/Practice Implications

Expand and deepen CTE opportunities, ensuring more students complete concentrator/completor pathways and take multiple courses (≥2–5).
Strengthen regional postsecondary connections, positioning 2-year institutions as central anchors for workforce retention.
Elevate sub-baccalaureate pathways as critical contributors to regional workforce strength.
Design retention strategies for 4-year graduates and high academic achievers, offering internships, research, and professional opportunities tied to local industries.
Target supports for vulnerable groups (low-income, SpecialEd, racial/ethnic subgroups) to reduce disconnection.
Maintain competitive local wages and employment opportunities to counter outward mobility and anchor graduates long-term.

In short, the models reaffirm that Southern Minnesota’s workforce is sustained by CTE and 2-year credentials, but retaining academically strong and 4-year graduates will require intentional strategies. Meanwhile, addressing equity gaps and economic competitiveness is essential to prevent long-term disconnection.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Prediction - post-secondary

Overall Model Performance
Across both dependent variables — postsecondary graduation location and highest credential earned — the pre-pruned CART models achieved accuracies of 61.7% and 64.2%, respectively. Both represented clear improvements over baseline distributions and showed that a relatively small set of predictors consistently explains meaningful variation in student pathways.
While not capturing all individual-level complexity, these models highlight distinct sets of academic, demographic, and experiential variables that shape whether students remain anchored in the Southern MN workforce pipeline or pursue mobility pathways.


Key Predictors Across Models
The following predictors emerged as the most consistently influential:

Academic readiness: MCA Reading and ACT Composite Score.
Economic status: Persistent disadvantages for low-income students.
Race/Ethnicity: White and Asian/PI students more likely to reach higher credentials; Black, AI, and Hispanic students more often concentrated in lower or incomplete outcomes.
PSEO participation: Steers students toward bachelor’s+ and out-of-region completions.
CTE engagement (courses taken): Reinforces regional and sub-baccalaureate pathways.

These predictors operate in two clear pipelines — one driving local attachment through sub-baccalaureate credentials, and one fostering mobility through advanced credentials.


Interpretation of Pathways

1. Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)

Regional completions clustered among economically disadvantaged students with moderate academic readiness.
Non-completion was strongly tied to low ACT and MCA scores, often regardless of background.
High academic readiness and PSEO participation predicted completions outside the region, fueling mobility pathways.

Implication: Regional institutions disproportionately serve disadvantaged students who achieve moderate readiness, while high scorers leave the region for completion.


2. Highest Credential Earned (highest.cred.level)

Bachelor’s or higher credentials were most strongly linked to high MCA and ACT scores, advantaged status, and PSEO participation.
Non-completion was almost guaranteed for students with low MCA Reading or ACT scores, even when other factors were favorable.
Associate or lower credentials (though less prominent in the tree structure) align with CTE-heavy pathways, serving as stabilizers for the regional workforce.

Implication: Academic readiness acts as the primary gateway to bachelor’s+ attainment, but economic and racial inequities remain barriers, even among high scorers.



Synthesis of Findings
Together, the models reinforce the existence of a dual-pipeline system in Southern Minnesota:

Regional Workforce Pipeline

Driven by CTE engagement, associate-or-lower credentials, and regional completions.
Anchors students with economic disadvantage and moderate readiness into the local labor market.
Provides workforce stability but limits long-term mobility and earning potential.

Mobility Pipeline

Driven by academic rigor, bachelor’s+ attainment, PSEO participation, and out-of-region completions.
Attracts advantaged, high-scoring students, who are least likely to remain in the region after completion.
Fuels statewide and out-of-state labor markets more than the local workforce.




Policy Implications

Strengthen regional anchors: Expand academic and financial supports for disadvantaged, moderate scorers to ensure successful completions in Southern MN institutions.
Address inequities in bachelor’s+ attainment: Target resources for high-achieving but low-income and underrepresented students to reduce barriers to advanced credentials.
Leverage CTE strategically: Maintain CTE as a stabilizer but ensure stackable pathways to prevent students from being locked into sub-associate outcomes.
Engage high-achievers locally: Create incentives and career opportunities that connect PSEO participants and bachelor’s+ completers back to the region to mitigate brain drain.



Conclusion
The predictive analysis confirms that academic readiness, economic status, and experiential factors like PSEO and CTE are the primary levers shaping postsecondary pathways. These pathways, in turn, determine whether students are most likely to remain in the Southern MN workforce or pursue mobility.
Ultimately, the models illustrate a structural duality: disadvantaged students with modest preparation form the backbone of the regional workforce through 2-year and regional completions, while advantaged high scorers are systematically funneled into statewide mobility. Policy efforts must therefore balance supporting the regional anchor pipeline with developing mechanisms to retain or re-engage mobile students after higher attainment.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Relationships - non-college grads
For non-college graduates, the central question is whether they secure meaningful employment in their home region. The evidence shows that regional employment is influenced most strongly by students’ accomplishments during high school, with demographics and local economic conditions playing secondary roles.
High school accomplishments stand out as the clearest drivers of regional employment. Career and Technical Education (CTE) is especially powerful: concentrators and students who take more CTE courses are consistently more likely to find meaningful regional work, and this advantage endures 10 years after graduation. Academic performance, measured by ACT and MCA scores, also matters. Lower scorers are more likely to transition earlier into the workforce, often finding employment in their home region. Higher scorers, by contrast, tend to pursue postsecondary education and eventually secure meaningful work elsewhere in Minnesota. PSEO participation provides an early push toward persistence and statewide opportunities, but it reduces the likelihood of staying in regional employment over time.
Demographics create important differences in access to regional work. Students in special education are far less likely to achieve meaningful regional employment and are instead overrepresented in non-meaningful work or disconnection. Economic status also plays a role: students from higher-income backgrounds are more likely to move into statewide opportunities, while lower-income peers are somewhat more concentrated in regional jobs, but also at higher risk of disconnection. Gender differences are small but consistent, with men more likely to be in meaningful regional jobs and women more often outside the regional workforce. Race and ethnicity show very modest overall effects; white graduates are slightly more likely to secure regional jobs compared to peers of color.
High school characteristics and local context shape the structure of opportunities available. Rural graduates are more likely to remain in meaningful regional employment, while urban graduates are more likely to move into Minnesota-wide jobs. County-level conditions matter: stronger local economies with lower unemployment and higher wages increase the chances that graduates find meaningful regional employment, while weaker counties increase the likelihood of disconnection. Regional (EDR) differences exist but are comparatively modest.
Taken together, the story is clear: for non-college graduates, CTE engagement is the most reliable path into meaningful employment in the region. Lower academic scorers and rural graduates are also more likely to remain rooted in local work, while higher academic achievers and those with early postsecondary exposure often leave the region for broader Minnesota opportunities. Demographics highlight groups at risk of missing out on regional work, and county conditions reveal where local economies either anchor graduates in meaningful jobs or push them toward disconnection.

Ranked Importance for Regional Employment (Most → Least)

CTE Engagement (Accomplishments: achievement + total courses) – strongest, most consistent predictor of meaningful regional work.
ACT & MCA Scores (Accomplishments) – lower scorers more likely to enter and remain in regional jobs; higher scorers more likely to leave the region.
Special Education Status (Demographic) – persistent disadvantage, much less likely to secure regional work.
Economic Status (Demographic) – lower-income grads somewhat more region-bound but also more disconnected; higher-income grads more mobile across MN.
PSEO Participation (Accomplishment) – reduces likelihood of regional employment over time as participants pursue statewide opportunities.
Rural/Urban (HS Characteristic) – rural grads more likely to stay in regional jobs; urban grads more likely to find work elsewhere in Minnesota.
County Conditions (Unemployment, Wages) – stronger local economies increase chances of regional employment.
Gender (Demographic) – men more likely in regional work; women more often outside.
Region (EDR) (HS Characteristic) – modest variation across Minnesota.
Race/Ethnicity (Demographic) – very small effects on regional employment.

👉 The headline story becomes: Among non-college graduates, the most dependable route into meaningful employment in the region is deep engagement with CTE. Regional jobs are also more common for lower scorers, rural students, and men, while higher scorers, PSEO participants, and higher-income students are more likely to move into statewide opportunities instead. Local economic conditions either anchor graduates in meaningful regional work or push them toward disconnection.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Prediction - non-college grads
This synthesis compares the three binary outcomes:

A: Regional vs. Statewide Meaningful Employment
B: Regional vs. Not Meaningful, Not Attending PS
C: Regional vs. No MN Employment Record, Not Attending PS

Model Performance Across Outcomes

A (Regional vs. Statewide): Accuracy levels were high (≈67–75%), consistently outperforming baseline. This reflects clearer separations in who stays local versus who is mobile within Minnesota.
B (Regional vs. Not Meaningful/No PS): Accuracy was modest (≈58–62%), slightly above baseline. Distinguishing meaningful local work from marginal attachment is harder, as both groups may share vulnerabilities.
C (Regional vs. No MN Record/No PS): Accuracy was moderate (≈56–62%), again above baseline but with declining lift over time. Predictors are strongest in the short-term, while long-term outcomes are harder to forecast from high school data.

Pattern: CART models are most powerful when contrasting regional stayers vs. statewide movers (A), and least predictive when comparing regional stayers vs. those completely disconnected (C at 10 years).

Key Predictors by Outcome

A (Regional vs. Statewide):
Race/Ethnicity, ACT Composite Score, MCA Reading, Economic Status, PSEO Participation.
Interpretation: Academic readiness and mobility pipelines (ACT, PSEO) drive statewide employment; regional employment is anchored by modest academic readiness and lower-income students.
B (Regional vs. Not Meaningful/No PS):
CTE Achievement, Total CTE Courses Taken, Race/Ethnicity, Special Education Status, ACT Composite Score.
Interpretation: CTE participation is the strongest shield against disconnection, while special education and race stratify risks.
C (Regional vs. No MN Record/No PS):
Total CTE Courses Taken, CTE Achievement, MCA Math/Reading, Race/Ethnicity, Special Education Status.
Interpretation: Depth in CTE is consistently protective; academic readiness matters differently over time (math at 1 year, ACT at 5 years, reading at 10). Racial and disability disparities persist.



Interpretation Over Time

Early (1 Year):

A: Modest ACT readiness and low-income students more likely to work regionally.
B: CTE engagement differentiates regional workers from those disconnected.
C: Math skills and ≥3 CTE courses are anchors; special education students face higher risks.

Mid-Term (5 Years):

A: ACT scores, race/ethnicity, and CTE sustain regional employment vs. statewide mobility.
B: CTE remains protective, but race/ethnicity and ACT readiness gain importance.
C: ACT, CTE, race, and income explain who stays regionally attached vs. who disconnects.

Long-Term (10 Years):

A: Regional employment stabilizes among low-income and modest academic performers; statewide employment aligns with higher scorers.
B: CTE depth still matters, but demographic inequities (race, special education) widen.
C: Reading proficiency and CTE achievement are decisive; racial disparities persist even with strong preparation.




Conclusion
Across all binaries:

CTE depth and achievement are the single most consistent predictors of regional employment — anchoring students early and protecting against both statewide mobility and disconnection.
Academic readiness matters, but the form shifts over time: math early, ACT in mid-term, reading in long-term.
Demographics stratify pathways: race/ethnicity, income, and special education status consistently increase disconnection risks or steer students away from regional employment.
Predictive power is strongest in Outcome A (mobility within MN) and weakest in Outcome C (long-term disconnection), reflecting how labor market forces dilute the predictive role of high school preparation over time.



Policy Implications

For A (Regional vs. Statewide): Retain high scorers and PSEO participants by connecting them to local opportunities, since they are most likely to leave the region.
For B (Regional vs. Not Meaningful/No PS): Expand CTE concentrator/completor opportunities and supports for special education students to prevent early disconnection.
For C (Regional vs. No MN Record/No PS): Ensure all students reach minimum academic thresholds in math and reading while expanding CTE access; supplement with long-term workforce equity initiatives to sustain regional employment.
Overall: The region’s workforce stability depends on expanding CTE depth, addressing academic readiness across subjects, and tackling inequities by race, income, and disability.

The original dataset provides whether the student was a basic participant, basic concentrator, basic completor, and/or a centrentrator 150 when taking a CTE course. It looks like each observation is unique by grade of the student. This means that one PersonID can have multiple observations.
In order to determine how I want to organize this data so that each observation represents the full characteristics of each PersonID I need to understand how these values are defined.

Basic Participant: Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes one or more state-approved CTE course(s).
Basic Concentrator: this is the old standard for years and required the student complete 240 hours. Any student successfully enrolled in a single CTE field for more than 240 hours (successful is defined as passing grade).
Basic Completor: any concentrator who attains academic and technical knowledge and skills and graduates from high school.
Concentrator 150: This is the new standard - Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes 150+ course hours (or more) as part of a state-approved secondary CTE program, within one career field.

Judging by these definitions, it seems that we will want three categories;

Those that participated in a CTE course but were not a concentrator or a completor, and
Those that participated in a CTE course and graduated as a concentrator.
Those that did not participate in a CTE course.

So essentially, filtering this dataset to provide the “highest level achieved” in terms of CTE coursework. We will focus on filtering this dataset to the highest level achieved and will then join with the graduate list which will have all the individuals that did not participate in any CTE courses.

section: Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Attendance (attended.ps)
text:
Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Attendance (attended.ps)
Across demographics, high school characteristics, and accomplishments, clear patterns emerge in who is most likely to pursue postsecondary education. Academic achievement and early exposure to postsecondary opportunities are the strongest predictors, while economic disadvantage and special education needs are the most powerful barriers. High school context measures show weaker associations, suggesting that student-level factors matter more than community background.


1. Strong Predictors of Postsecondary Attendance
These variables show strong or moderate associations and consistently differentiate postsecondary attendance outcomes.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




MCA Reading, Math, Science
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher MCA scores strongly predict postsecondary attendance, with Reading the single strongest indicator.


ACTCompositeScore
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher ACT scores significantly increase likelihood of attending PS.


pseo.participant
Accomplishment (categorical)
Participation in PSEO strongly boosts PS attendance, highlighting the value of early postsecondary exposure.


SpecialEdStatus
Demographic
Students in special education are far less likely to attend PS, making this one of the most powerful barriers.


Economic Status
Demographic
Low-income students are much less likely to attend PS, showing persistent socioeconomic disparities.






2. Moderate Predictors — Secondary but Meaningful
These variables show moderate or weaker effects, useful for understanding disparities but less decisive than the strongest predictors.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




RaceEthnicity
Demographic
White and Asian/PI students most likely to attend PS; Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students less likely.


Gender
Demographic
Females somewhat more likely to attend PS than males, but the gap is modest.


total.cte.courses.taken
Accomplishment (continuous)
Taking more CTE courses correlates with higher PS attendance, but effect is modest compared to academics.






3. Weak or Inconsistent Predictors — Limited Value
These variables show weak associations and are less useful in predicting postsecondary attendance independently.








Variable
Type
Notes




cte.achievement
Accomplishment (categorical)
Little difference across CTE participants, concentrators, or non-participants in terms of PS attendance.


Dem_Desc
HS Characteristic
Urban, rural, and mixed settings show almost no independent effect on PS attendance.


avg.unemp.rate
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Significant differences observed, but effect size small; stronger economies modestly raise PS attendance.


avg.wages.pct.state
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Higher relative local wages linked to higher PS attendance, though weaker than unemployment rate differences.






Conclusion
The most consistent predictors of postsecondary attendance are academic achievement (MCA and ACT scores), PSEO participation, and demographic disadvantages (special education and low-income status). Race, gender, and CTE course-taking add nuance but are secondary factors. High school context measures such as community type, local unemployment, and local wages matter less than individual-level academic and demographic characteristics.
In short: academic readiness and early exposure to college drive postsecondary entry, while economic disadvantage and special education needs are the greatest barriers.

Cramer’s V Scores and Strength

SpecialEdStatus: V = 0.288 → Moderate-to-Strong association
Economic Status: V = 0.218 → Moderate association

Gender: V = 0.118 → Weak association

Ranking (strongest to weakest):

SpecialEdStatus (0.288)
Economic Status (0.218)
RaceEthnicity (0.150)
Gender (0.118)




Interpretation of Results

SpecialEdStatus: Students in special education are substantially less likely to attend postsecondary. The split is stark: most non-SPED students go on, while nearly two-thirds of SPED students do not. This makes it the most powerful demographic predictor.
Economic Status: Low-income students are much less likely to attend postsecondary compared to their non-low-income peers. The difference is meaningful but smaller than SPED.
RaceEthnicity: Attendance patterns vary by group. White and Asian/PI students show the highest participation, while American Indian, Hispanic, and Black students are less likely to attend. Disparities are clear but not as large as the income and SPED gaps.
Gender: Females are somewhat more likely to attend postsecondary than males, but the effect is weaker compared to other demographics.




Conclusion
Among demographic factors, special education status and economic status are the strongest predictors of postsecondary attendance, both showing moderate effect sizes. Race/ethnicity matters, with persistent gaps across groups, but its predictive strength is weaker. Gender plays only a minor role, with females more likely to attend but not dramatically so.
In short: SPED and income disadvantage most strongly limit postsecondary access, while racial/ethnic disparities and gender patterns play secondary roles.

High School Characteristics

Dem_Desc

Cramer’s V / ANOVA Results

Dem_Desc: V = 0.039 → Very weak association
avg.unemp.rate: F = 484.36, p < 0.001 → Significant difference, but effect size likely small
avg.wages.pct.state: F = 269.68, p < 0.001 → Significant difference, but effect size likely small

Ranking (strongest to weakest):

avg.unemp.rate (most statistically significant mean difference)
avg.wages.pct.state (significant but smaller than unemployment)
Dem_Desc (essentially negligible association)




Interpretation of Results

Dem_Desc: Urban, rural, and mixed community contexts show little independent relationship to postsecondary attendance once other factors are considered. Students from all community types attend at broadly similar rates.
avg.unemp.rate: Students in counties with lower unemployment rates are significantly more likely to attend postsecondary. This suggests stronger local labor markets reduce immediate employment pressure and encourage PS attendance.
avg.wages.pct.state: Higher local wages (relative to state average) are also linked to higher PS attendance, though the effect is weaker than unemployment. Better local economic conditions appear to create more postsecondary participation.




Conclusion
High school context measures show weak-to-modest associations with postsecondary attendance. Local economic indicators (unemployment and wages) matter more than rural/urban community type, suggesting economic opportunity environments influence whether students pursue college. However, compared to demographic factors like special education and income status, these contextual factors are secondary predictors.

section: Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)
text:
Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)
Across demographics, high school characteristics, and accomplishments, the clearest pattern is that academic achievement and demographic disadvantage drive postsecondary completion outcomes. Strong test performance and higher ACT scores substantially increase graduation odds, while racial/ethnic disparities, income barriers, and special education needs sharply reduce them. High school contextual factors (economic environment, rural/urban setting) play a smaller but still significant role.


1. Strong Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation
These variables show moderate-to-strong associations and consistently differentiate who graduates from postsecondary institutions.

Type
Key Insights




RaceEthnicity

Economic Status

SpecialEdStatus
Demographic
Students in special education graduate at much lower rates than non-SPED peers.

Higher ACT scores strongly predict graduation.


MCA Reading, Math, Science
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher MCA scores strongly predict graduation, with Reading as the single strongest signal.






2. Moderate Predictors — Secondary but Meaningful
These variables show modest effects on graduation, adding nuance but not as decisive as the strongest predictors.

CTE concentrators/completors graduate at slightly higher rates, but overall effect is weak-to-moderate.


avg.unemp.rate

Lower local unemployment modestly improves graduation rates.


avg.wages.pct.state

Higher relative local wages modestly improve graduation rates.






3. Weak or Inconsistent Predictors — Limited Value
These variables show weak associations and add little predictive value independently.








Variable
Type

Dem_Desc

Community type (urban, rural, mixed) shows negligible independent impact on graduation once other factors are considered.






Conclusion
The most consistent predictors of postsecondary graduation are academic performance (MCA and ACT scores) and demographic disadvantages (race/ethnicity, economic status, special education needs). Gender and CTE measures add modest explanatory value, while high school context factors like unemployment and wages are statistically significant but secondary.
In short: graduation depends heavily on academic readiness and overcoming demographic barriers, with local context and programmatic engagement (CTE) playing smaller supporting roles.

title: Post-secondary pathways
section: Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation by Institution Sector (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)
text:
Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation by Institution Sector (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)
Graduates sort into public 4-year colleges, public 2-year colleges, or other types of institutions along clear demographic and academic lines. The strongest pattern is that academic rigor and early college exposure (PSEO) channel students into 4-year pathways, while CTE engagement and demographic disadvantage channel students into 2-year pathways. Since prior findings show that 2-year credentials are more strongly tied to meaningful regional employment, this sorting mechanism has direct implications for regional workforce retention.


1. Strong Predictors of Institution Sector
These variables show moderate associations or strong academic effects and consistently distinguish graduates of 2-year versus 4-year institutions.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




SpecialEdStatus
Demographic
SPED students disproportionately graduate from 2-year colleges, rarely from 4-year institutions.


Economic Status
Demographic
Low-income students more likely to graduate from 2-year colleges; non–low-income students dominate 4-year completions.


ACTCompositeScore
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher ACT scores strongly linked to 4-year graduation; lower scores linked to 2-year institutions.


MCA Reading, Math, Science
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher MCA scores drive 4-year outcomes; lower scores concentrate in 2-year institutions.


PSEO Participation
Accomplishment (categorical)
Students who participated in PSEO disproportionately graduate from 4-year colleges, reinforcing early exposure to rigorous pathways.






2. Moderate Predictors — Secondary but Meaningful
These variables show moderate associations, adding nuance to institutional sorting.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




RaceEthnicity
Demographic
White and Asian/PI students are more likely to complete at 4-year institutions, while Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students are more concentrated in 2-year outcomes.


Gender
Demographic
Females somewhat more likely to graduate from 4-year institutions; males more represented in 2-year outcomes.


total.cte.courses.taken
Accomplishment (continuous)
More CTE courses increase the likelihood of 2-year completions.


cte.achievement
Accomplishment (categorical)
CTE concentrators/completors disproportionately complete at 2-year institutions.


avg.unemp.rate
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Students from higher unemployment counties lean toward 2-year outcomes.


avg.wages.pct.state
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Lower-wage areas are associated with more 2-year completions.






3. Weak Predictors — Limited Independent Effect








Variable
Type
Notes




Dem_Desc
HS Characteristic
Community type (urban/rural/mixed) shows only weak effects once demographics and academics are accounted for.






Conclusion
Institutional sorting reflects a dual system:

High academic achievers and PSEO participants are channeled into 4-year institutions, a pathway associated with statewide mobility and weaker regional retention.
Students facing economic disadvantage, SPED identification, or strong CTE engagement are more likely to graduate from 2-year colleges, a pathway tied to higher odds of meaningful employment within the region.

In short: Institution sector is not only a reflection of student preparation and background, but also a mechanism that shapes regional workforce outcomes. By understanding these predictors, policymakers can strengthen 2-year college pathways as engines of regional employment, while ensuring disadvantaged groups are supported in persisting and completing their chosen pathways.

Interpretation of Results

SpecialEdStatus: Students in special education are disproportionately represented in public 2-year colleges, with much smaller shares in 4-year institutions. Non-SPED students are more likely to graduate from 4-year institutions.
Economic Status: Low-income students are more likely to graduate from public 2-year colleges and less likely from 4-year institutions compared to their non–low-income peers.
RaceEthnicity: Disparities are evident. White and Asian/PI students are more likely to graduate from 4-year institutions, while Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students show greater representation in 2-year institutions.
Gender: Females are more likely to graduate from 4-year institutions than males, while males are slightly more represented in 2-year pathways.




Conclusion
The type of postsecondary institution students graduate from is most strongly associated with special education status and economic status, followed by race/ethnicity and gender. Disadvantaged groups (SPED, low-income, and historically marginalized racial/ethnic groups) are more likely to complete at 2-year colleges, while more advantaged peers and females are more likely to graduate from 4-year institutions.
In short: institutional sector of graduation reflects both opportunity and constraint — disadvantaged students often cluster into public 2-year colleges, while advantaged students disproportionately graduate from 4-year institutions.

Conclusion
High school contextual factors show statistically significant but modest effects on the type of postsecondary institution where students graduate. Local economic conditions (unemployment and wages) matter more than rural/urban school setting, nudging students toward either 2-year or 4-year completions. However, compared to demographic and accomplishment factors, these remain secondary predictors of institutional sector outcomes.

Higher academic scores (ACT, MCA) push students toward 4-year institutions.
CTE pathways (courses, concentrator status) push students toward 2-year institutions.
PSEO participation nudges students toward 4-year completions.

In short: rigor and PSEO align with 4-year outcomes, while CTE aligns with 2-year outcomes, highlighting a clear sorting mechanism between academic and applied postsecondary pathways.

title: Post-secondary pathways
section: Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation by Location (ps.grad.location)
text:
Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Graduation by Location (ps.grad.location)
Graduates sort into three categories: Southern MN completions, Minnesota outside the region, and out-of-state completions. The clearest pattern is that demographic disadvantage and CTE engagement anchor students regionally, while academic rigor and PSEO participation propel students toward mobility. This sorting mechanism directly ties to workforce outcomes: regional completions are most strongly linked to meaningful employment in Southern MN, while out-of-region completions align with statewide mobility.


1. Strong Predictors of Graduation Location
These variables show the strongest and most consistent differentiation between regional and out-of-region completions.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




Economic Status
Demographic
Low-income students disproportionately graduate in Southern MN; non–low-income peers dominate out-of-region completions.


ACTCompositeScore
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher scores drive out-of-region completions; lower scores align with regional completions.


MCA Reading, Math, Science
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher MCA scores align with out-of-region completions; lower scores with regional completions.


CTE Achievement & Courses Taken
Accomplishment
CTE concentrators and students with more CTE courses are disproportionately represented in Southern MN completions, anchoring them locally.






2. Moderate Predictors — Secondary but Meaningful
These variables show modest but still meaningful associations.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




RaceEthnicity
Demographic
White and Asian/PI graduates more likely to complete outside the region; Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students more concentrated in regional completions.


SpecialEdStatus
Demographic
SPED students are more likely to complete in Southern MN, with fewer out-of-region completions.


PSEO Participation
Accomplishment
PSEO students lean toward out-of-region completions, reinforcing the program’s tie to 4-year pathways.


avg.wages.pct.state
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Graduates from lower-wage counties are more anchored to Southern MN completions; higher-wage counties produce more out-of-region completers.


avg.unemp.rate
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Higher unemployment areas modestly increase the likelihood of regional completions.






3. Weak Predictors — Limited Independent Effect








Variable
Type
Notes




Gender
Demographic
Male and female students show negligible differences in graduation location.


Dem_Desc
HS Characteristic
Urban/rural/mixed school context adds little explanatory power once other factors are considered.






Conclusion
Graduation location reflects a dual system:

Academic rigor (high ACT/MCA scores, PSEO) sorts students into out-of-region completions, fueling statewide mobility.
CTE engagement, low-income status, SPED identification, and disadvantaged local economies anchor students into Southern MN completions, tying them to the regional workforce.

In short: regional completions are the strongest predictor of regional workforce retention, and these are most common among students facing economic or educational disadvantage and those engaged in CTE. Strengthening supports for these students can help ensure their regional degrees translate into long-term, meaningful employment in Southern Minnesota.

Gender (0.011)




Interpretation of Results

Economic Status: Low-income graduates are more concentrated in Southern MN completions, while non–low-income students are more represented in Minnesota outside the region and especially out-of-state completions. This highlights income as the key factor anchoring students to the regional workforce.
RaceEthnicity: White and Asian/PI students are somewhat more likely to graduate outside the region (both MN and out-of-state). Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students are more concentrated in regional completions, suggesting stronger local ties despite overall smaller representation in PS completion.
SpecialEdStatus: SPED students are more likely to graduate in Southern MN, with far fewer completions outside the region, reflecting constrained mobility.
Gender: Male and female students show nearly identical distributions across institution locations, with negligible differences.




Conclusion
Economic status is the clearest demographic predictor of where students graduate, with low-income students more anchored to regional completions and advantaged peers more mobile, graduating outside the region or state. Race/ethnicity and SPED status show weaker effects but similarly indicate that disadvantaged groups are more likely to stay regional. Gender plays no meaningful role.
In short: demographic disadvantage corresponds to stronger regional attachment through local completions, while more advantaged groups are more mobile, graduating outside the region. This reinforces prior findings that regional retention and workforce stability are most tied to pathways serving low-income and special education students.

Conclusion
High school context measures show that local economic strength influences postsecondary graduation location more than rural/urban school setting. Students from stronger wage environments are more mobile, completing outside the region, while those from lower-wage areas are anchored in Southern MN institutions. This supports the broader pattern that regional retention is tied to constrained opportunity environments, while advantaged areas encourage mobility.

High school accomplishments divide students between regional and mobile pathways.

Higher academic achievement (ACT, MCA) and PSEO participation align with out-of-region completions, fueling statewide or national mobility.
CTE engagement is linked to regional completions in Southern MN, anchoring students more tightly to the local workforce.

title: Post-secondary pathways
section: Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Highest Credential Attainment (highest.cred.level)
text:
Total Summary: Predictors of Postsecondary Highest Credential Attainment (highest.cred.level)
Students diverge across credential levels — no college, some college, sub-associate, associate, and bachelor’s or higher — along clear demographic, academic, and programmatic lines. The strongest pattern is that academic rigor and PSEO participation drive bachelor’s attainment and mobility, while economic disadvantage, special education needs, and CTE engagement steer students toward sub-baccalaureate or associate pathways. This has direct implications for regional workforce development, since sub-baccalaureate and associate completions are most strongly tied to meaningful employment in Southern MN.


1. Strong Predictors of Credential Level
These variables show moderate to strong associations and consistently differentiate between bachelor’s-or-higher versus sub-baccalaureate outcomes.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




SpecialEdStatus
Demographic
SPED students overwhelmingly concentrated in no college or sub-associate levels, rarely achieving bachelor’s or higher.


Economic Status
Demographic
Low-income students disproportionately in sub-associate and no-college categories; non–low-income peers dominate higher degrees.


ACTCompositeScore
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher scores strongly linked to bachelor’s or higher attainment.


MCA Reading, Math, Science
Accomplishment (continuous)
Higher MCA scores correlate with bachelor’s attainment; lower scores with associate or less.


PSEO Participation
Accomplishment (categorical)
PSEO students far more likely to reach bachelor’s or higher, reinforcing early college exposure as a pipeline to advanced credentials.






2. Moderate Predictors — Secondary but Meaningful
These variables add important nuance but have weaker overall effects.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




RaceEthnicity
Demographic
White and Asian/PI students more likely to reach bachelor’s or higher; Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students concentrated in lower-credential categories.


Gender
Demographic
Females more likely to achieve bachelor’s or higher, while males are more often in sub-associate categories.


total.cte.courses.taken
Accomplishment (continuous)
More CTE courses link to higher rates of associate attainment, less often bachelor’s.


cte.achievement
Accomplishment (categorical)
CTE concentrators/completors most likely to earn associate degrees, with lower bachelor’s representation.


avg.unemp.rate
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Higher unemployment counties see lower bachelor’s attainment, more sub-associate outcomes.


avg.wages.pct.state
HS Characteristic (continuous)
Higher-wage counties foster greater bachelor’s attainment; lower-wage areas cluster in associate or less.






3. Weak Predictors — Limited Independent Effect








Variable
Type
Notes




Dem_Desc
HS Characteristic
Urban/rural/mixed school setting shows only weak differences once other factors are considered.






Conclusion
Credential attainment reflects a stratified system:

Academic rigor and PSEO participation drive bachelor’s and higher attainment, fueling pathways to statewide or out-of-state mobility.
CTE engagement, low-income status, SPED identification, and disadvantaged local economies anchor students in associate or sub-associate outcomes, which are most strongly tied to regional workforce retention.

In short: the highest credential earned is powerfully shaped by both individual disadvantage and academic preparation. While bachelor’s-or-higher degrees signal mobility, associate pathways linked to CTE and disadvantage markers remain the backbone of regional employment in Southern MN.

Interpretation of Results

Economic Status: Low-income students are less likely to achieve a bachelor’s or higher credential, and more likely to stop at no college or sub-associate levels. Non–low-income students dominate higher credential attainment.
RaceEthnicity: Racial gaps are clear. White and Asian/PI students are much more likely to earn a bachelor’s degree or higher, while Black, Hispanic, and American Indian students are more concentrated in no college, some college, or sub-associate levels.
Gender: Females are somewhat more likely to achieve a bachelor’s or higher, while males are more represented in no college or less than associate levels. Differences are meaningful but smaller than income or SPED status.




Conclusion
Highest credential level is strongly patterned by disadvantage markers.

SpecialEdStatus and economic status are the most powerful predictors, with SPED and low-income students disproportionately clustered in lower-credential outcomes.
Race/ethnicity shows persistent gaps, with historically marginalized groups less likely to achieve higher degrees.
Gender plays a smaller but notable role, with females outperforming males in bachelor’s and higher attainment.

In short: the pathway to higher credentials is strongly stratified by socioeconomic, racial, and special education factors, shaping long-term employment opportunities and mobility.

Conclusion
High school contextual factors matter modestly for highest credential attainment. Local economic conditions (unemployment, wages) are more influential than school setting, with stronger local economies tied to higher credential levels. Still, their predictive power remains weaker compared to demographic factors like SPED status, income, and race/ethnicity.
In short: economic context nudges students toward or away from higher credentials, but individual-level disadvantage remains the dominant factor shaping credential attainment.

cte.achievement (weak-to-moderate categorical effect)




Interpretation of Results

Academic Rigor (ACT & MCA scores): Students with higher test scores are overwhelmingly more likely to achieve a bachelor’s degree or higher. Lower-scoring students cluster in associate or less-than-associate categories, underscoring academic preparation as the single strongest determinant of credential level.
PSEO Participation: Students who engaged in PSEO are much more likely to earn a bachelor’s or higher degree, reflecting the program’s alignment with rigorous, transfer-oriented pathways.
CTE Engagement (cte.achievement & total courses): CTE concentrators and students taking more CTE courses are more likely to earn associate degrees or some college, and less likely to reach the bachelor’s level. This reflects the program’s orientation toward applied, shorter-term credentials.




Conclusion
Highest credential level is primarily driven by academic rigor (ACT and MCA scores) and secondarily by PSEO participation. Students with stronger academics and early college exposure reach bachelor’s or higher degrees at far greater rates. In contrast, CTE engagement correlates with associate-level attainment, reinforcing its role as an anchor to regional workforce pathways rather than extended academic pipelines.
In short: academic rigor and PSEO push students upward into bachelor’s and beyond, while CTE steers students toward sub-baccalaureate credentials, aligning with the regional employment advantage of 2-year pathways.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
1. Attending Postsecondary Education

Key Predictors: Economic status (low-income less likely to attend), race/ethnicity (persistent gaps), and special education status (lower attendance).
Takeaway: Disadvantaged students are disproportionately less likely to enroll in PS at all, putting them at high risk of long-term disconnection.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
2. Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)

Key Predictors: Economic status and SPED remain barriers to completion; racial gaps persist; academic readiness improves odds of graduating.
Takeaway: Simply completing PS dramatically reduces disconnection and boosts employment. Non-completers remain the most vulnerable group in the workforce pipeline.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
3. Institution Sector of Graduation (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)

Key Predictors:

Academic rigor and PSEO → 4-year completions.
CTE engagement, SPED, and low-income → 2-year completions.

Takeaway: Institution type sorts students into applied versus academic pathways. Since 2-year completions are more strongly tied to regional employment, CTE and disadvantage groups inadvertently form the backbone of Southern MN’s workforce, while academically strong students pursue more mobile 4-year pathways.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
4. Location of Graduation (ps.grad.location)

Key Predictors:

Disadvantaged students (low-income, SPED, marginalized race/ethnicity) → more likely to graduate in Southern MN.
High scorers and PSEO participants → more likely to graduate outside the region (other MN or out-of-state).
Local economic conditions (lower wages, higher unemployment) → stronger Southern MN completions.

Takeaway: Regional completions are most common among disadvantaged groups and CTE students, reinforcing their role in regional workforce stability.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
5. Highest Credential Earned (highest.cred.level)

Key Predictors:

Academic rigor (ACT, MCA) and PSEO → bachelor’s or higher.
CTE engagement, low-income, SPED, disadvantaged counties → associate or sub-associate.

Takeaway: Credential level is the clearest stratifier of opportunity. Bachelor’s+ aligns with mobility, while associate/sub-associate aligns with regional employment.



Overall Conclusion
The postsecondary pipeline is shaped by two reinforcing forces:

Mobility Pipeline:

Driven by academic rigor and PSEO.
Leads to 4-year+ degrees, completions outside the region, and statewide mobility.
Most common among advantaged, higher-scoring students.

Regional Pipeline:

Driven by CTE engagement, 2-year institutions, economic disadvantage, SPED, and lower-wage/unemployment counties.
Leads to associate/sub-associate degrees and Southern MN completions, strongly tied to meaningful regional employment.
Most common among disadvantaged students who remain anchored locally.


In short: Southern MN’s workforce stability relies heavily on the regional pipeline of 2-year and CTE-driven pathways, which disproportionately serve low-income and SPED students. Meanwhile, academically strong and advantaged students pursue 4-year and higher credentials, fueling statewide and out-of-state mobility.
Policy Implication: To strengthen the regional workforce, interventions should both (1) support disadvantaged students in completing and leveraging their 2-year pathways and (2) create incentives for academically strong students to remain engaged in the region after completing higher degrees.

title: CTEEnrollment
text:
The next dataset is individuals that were enrolled in CTE courses. I’m first going to load the entire dataset, then clean it up, and then I will merge it with my master/Southern graduate dataset.


cte.enrollment.original <- read_csv('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/CTEEnrollment/CTEEnrollment.csv') %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  filter(FiscalYearTimeID != "NULL") %>%
  mutate(CareerCluster = ifelse(CareerCluster == "26" & CareerClusterName == "Diversified Youth Apprenticeship", "25", CareerCluster),
         CareerCluster = ifelse(CareerCluster == "NULL", "0", CareerCluster),
         CareerCluster = str_replace(CareerCluster, "Design", "11"),
         CareerCluster = as.integer(CareerCluster))


career.cluster.codes.names.original <- read_xlsx('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/CTEEnrollment/career-cluster-codes-names_from SLEDS_March2025.xlsx') %>%
  mutate(cte.year = ifelse(Introduced > 2020, 2021, Discontinued),
         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(Introduced) & is.na(Discontinued), 2021, cte.year),
         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(cte.year), 2020, cte.year),
         CareerClusterName.new = as_factor(CareerClusterName.new))


career.cluster.codes.names.addendum <- data.frame(`CareerCluster` = c(0, 1, 2),
                                                  CareerClusterName.new = c("NULL", "Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources", "Architecture & Construction"),
                                                  Status = c("Retired", "Retired", "Retired"),
                                                  Introduced = c(2021, 2021, 2021),
                                                  Discontinued = c(2021, 2021, 2021),
                                                  cte.year = c(2020, 2020, 2020))

career.cluster.codes.names <- career.cluster.codes.names.original %>%
  rbind(career.cluster.codes.names.addendum)

cte.enrollment.master <- cte.enrollment.original %>%
  mutate(year = str_sub(FiscalYearTimeID, 1, 4),
         year = as.integer(year),
         cte.year = ifelse(year < 2021, 2020, 2021)) %>%
  left_join(career.cluster.codes.names[,c(1,2,6)], by = c("CareerCluster", "cte.year")) %>%
  select(-CareerClusterName, -year, -cte.year) %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerClusterName.new)

There seems to be a minor coding error in the careercluster column. For one particular class, it was consistently labeled “Information Technology” even though the field requires a number value. In addition, “information Technology” doesn’t seem to match the course due to the following information;
Program Course Name: Family and Consumer Science Course title: Apparrel CareerCluster: Design CareerClusterName: 6 (which should be a letter value, not a code).

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student
text:
Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student

We’ll start with summarising the number of cte courses the observations have taken.
The tables below show that the average number of CTE courses taken by all PersonID in the master dataset is 4.01 with a standard deviation of +/-3.41. This is a high standard deviation meaning there are values quite far from the mean.
The second row of the table shows the average number of CTE courses taken by individuals who took at least one CTE course. The average jumps up a bit to 4.65 with a standard deviation of 3.24.








Below is a chart showing the distribution of CTE courses taken by individuals. This shows that a a large majority of students take 10 courses or less.








Up next is to see if the percentage of students taking a CTE course varies significantly by RUCA group.
There is a significant difference in whether a student has taken at least one CTE course and their high school county RUCA category. Although 84% of all graduates took at least one CTE course, that percentage is highest in town/rural mix counties with 90% where as the other two RUCA categories had 85%.
Of those students that took at least 1 CTE course, the average number of CTE courses taken ranged from 5.1 in our entirely urban districts to 4.6 in town/rural mix districts.
The mean and medians also show significant difference. The more rural a district is, the higher average number of CTE courses taken by students - 5 for town/rural mix districts compared to 4.3 for entirely urban.

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
text:
Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
Let’s dig into the breadth of CTE course concentrations a graduate would take by looking at the proportion of graduates that took at least one course within a concentration.
The table below shows that a third of all graduates took a CTE course in Transportation, Distribution & Logistics, and agriculture, food and natural resources, followed by 32% in Human Services, and a quarter in Health science and Business, Management and Administrative.


cte.cf.prop <- master.4 %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  mutate(cte.cf.taken = ifelse(n.courses > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  tabyl(CareerCluster, cte.cf.taken) %>%
  mutate(pct.taken.cf = Yes / (Yes + No)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(pct.taken.cf))

datatable(cte.cf.prop, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  formatCurrency(2:3, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(4)






Now we will take a look at the breakdown of the number of times a CTE courses has been taken within a CareerCluster for each PersonID. I expect there to be a lot of variation in this data since different schools might focus on different types of CTE offerings depending on the local employment makeup.
First, lets look at the concentrations of courses taken across CareerClusters.
Surprisingly, agriculture, food and natural resources was the careercluster with the highest percentage of courses taken with 22.4%. This was followed by transportation, distribution and logistics with 13.3% and human services with 12.3%.








Lets see how this looks broken down by county.
The county maps do show some differences in percentages across career clusters. Agriculture, food and natural resources had higher percentages taken in the more rural counties. The more urban counties had higher percentages of health science and human services.

We have 5,744,192 rows and 5 columns in this dataset. Here are the descriptions for each of the columns.

K12AsstTimeID: Day, month, and year the assessment took place.
TestName: Name of the test taken. There are 12 different tests in the dataset -

ACCESS: English proficiency,
ALTACCESS: English proficiency for special education or meet requirements
MCA-II & MCA-III: Minnesota Comprehsensive Assessments (series 2 and 3)
MOD-II, MOD-III: Modified Comprehensive Assessment, used only until 2014
MTAS & MTAS-III: Minnesota Test of Academic Skills
MTELL: an alternate assessment for students learning English (like the MTAS or MOD). MTELL was only administered from 2007-2010 during the series-II of MCAs.
SOLOM: Minnesota Student Oral Language Observation Matrix
TEAE: one of two assessments that Minnesota used to meet the requirements to test ELs in all four domains of language (the other was SOLOM). TEAE was used 2002 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012. SOLOM was used 2004 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012.

Subject: Classifies each test that is given to a student based on the areas measured. There are 8 factors;

A: Aural (listening) - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
C: Composite - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
L: Listening/Speaking
M: Math
O: Oral - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
R: Reading
S: Science
W: Writing

GradeTested: Grade student was enrolled in when performing assessment.
AchievementLevel: Used to count the number of students in each achievement level by group such as race, gender, and ethnicity. It must be calculated from other students at a similar graden and subject for a specific year.

ACCESS students are graded on a language proficiency scale of 1 through 6.
ALT-ACCESS students are graded using a P1 through P3 and A1 through A3 scale.
There are 4 different levels for the MCA test

D: Does not meet standards
E: Exceeds standards
M: Meets Standards
P: Partially meets standards

SOLOM tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest
TEAE tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest.


There are two ways in which we are going to code our graduates.
The first is to identify whether a student has been identified as an English learner. This means filtering students that have taken the ACCESS, ALT-ACCESS, MTELL, MTAS, TEAE, MOD-II, MOD-III, or SOLOM at least once in their career.
The second is be determining their highest achievement level in each subject of the MCA tests within the dataset. The dataset provides each instance of a test for each student so many are students are listed numerous times - once for each time they took a test.
Lets do this in two separate files and then join each with the master file.
Starting with identifying the EL students.


el <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(!TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(english.learner = 1)

This dataset identified 34,995 individuals who were identified as an english learner at least one time in the original dataset.
Now we will determine the highest achievement level for each subject for each student.


mca <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevel != "NULL") %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(AchievementLevelCode = ifelse(AchievementLevel == "D", 1,
                                       ifelse(AchievementLevel == "P", 2,
                                              ifelse(AchievementLevel == "M", 3, 4))))

mca.highest <- mca %>%
  group_by(PersonID, Subject) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevelCode == max(AchievementLevelCode)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, Subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(mca.subject = paste("MCA.", Subject, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, mca.subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(id = seq(n())) %>%
  spread(key = mca.subject, value = AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(MCA.M, .direction = c("downup")) %>%
  fill(MCA.R, .direction = "downup") %>%
  fill(MCA.S, .direction = "downup") %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-id)

  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%

         Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Town/rural mix", "Urban/town/rural mix", "Entirely urban"))

  left_join(mca.highest, by = "PersonID") %>%
